_note: DEMO CORPUS. Short paraphrased excerpts written for this project's demo patients (type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension). They summarize the named public guidelines but are NOT verbatim quotations and have not been clinically reviewed; verify against the source document before any clinical use. Each chunk carries its source and section so citations stay traceable.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.text: A reasonable A1C goal for many nonpregnant adults with diabetes is below 7% if it can be reached safely without significant hypoglycemia. Less stringent goals may be appropriate for patients with limited life expectancy, advanced complications, or high hypoglycemia risk.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.text: Measure A1C at least twice a year in patients who are meeting treatment goals with stable glycemia, and at least quarterly in patients whose therapy has changed or who are not meeting glycemic goals.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.text: Diabetes can be diagnosed by an A1C of 6.5% or higher, a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, or a 2-hour plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher during an oral glucose tolerance test. In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, results should be confirmed on repeat testing.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.text: Metformin, when not contraindicated and tolerated, is the preferred initial pharmacologic agent for type 2 diabetes. When A1C remains above goal, consider adding agents; those with proven cardiovascular or kidney benefit are favored in patients with established atherosclerotic disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.text: Long-term metformin use can be associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. Periodic measurement of B12 should be considered, particularly in patients with anemia or peripheral neuropathy.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.section: Chronic Kidney Disease and Risk Management
chunks.text: In people with type 2 diabetes, screen for chronic kidney disease at least annually with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and an estimated glomerular filtration rate.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.section: Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Hypertension
chunks.text: For people with diabetes and hypertension, a blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg is recommended if it can be safely attained.

chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
chunks.section: Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Lipid Management
chunks.text: For people with diabetes aged 40 to 75 years without established atherosclerotic disease, use moderate-intensity statin therapy in addition to lifestyle therapy. High-intensity statin therapy is reasonable when additional cardiovascular risk factors are present.

chunks.source: ACC/AHA Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol
chunks.text: In adults aged 40 to 75 years with diabetes and an LDL cholesterol of 70 to 189 mg/dL, moderate-intensity statin therapy is recommended. In those with multiple risk factors, high-intensity statin therapy to lower LDL cholesterol by at least 50 percent is reasonable.

chunks.source: ACC/AHA Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol
chunks.text: Assess adherence and the LDL cholesterol response 4 to 12 weeks after starting or adjusting statin therapy, then every 3 to 12 months as needed.

chunks.source: ACC/AHA Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol
chunks.text: Fasting triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or higher are elevated. In adults with persistently elevated triglycerides, evaluate for secondary causes such as poor glycemic control, obesity, and medications before adding triglyceride-lowering therapy. Triglycerides of 500 mg/dL or higher carry a risk of pancreatitis and warrant more urgent treatment.

chunks.source: ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults
chunks.text: In adults with hypertension and diabetes, begin antihypertensive drug treatment at a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg or higher, with a treatment goal below 130/80 mmHg.

chunks.source: ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults
chunks.text: First-line antihypertensive agents include thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers. ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers are reasonable in patients with diabetes and albuminuria.

chunks.source: ACC/AHA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults
chunks.text: Adults starting or adjusting antihypertensive therapy should be reassessed monthly until blood pressure control is achieved.
